questionText:
Read the following excerpt on Nandalal Bose and the illumination of the Indian Constitution and answer the questions:

When the Constituent Assembly of India completed drafting the Constitution of the Republic of India, Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru personally invited Nandalal Bose and his master students from Kala Bhavana, Santiniketan, to illustrate the original calligraphed manuscript. Working between 1949 and 1950, Nandalal executed 22 monumental header panels for the 22 parts of the Constitution, visually chronicling 5,000 years of Indian civilizational history. Each illustration was carefully chosen to reflect the spirit of the corresponding constitutional text: Part III on Fundamental Rights is headed by Lord Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana returning victoriously to Ayodhya; Part IV on Directive Principles of State Policy depicts Lord Krishna preaching the Bhagavad Gita to Arjuna on the battlefield; and other sections feature seals from the Indus Valley Civilization, the Vedic ashram, Gautam Buddha, Lord Mahavira, Emperor Ashoka, Emperor Akbar, Chhatrapati Shivaji, Rani Lakshmibai, Mahatma Gandhi's Dandi March, and Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose.

questionText:
Read the following excerpt on the statutory Flag Code, proportions, and symbolism of the National Flag and answer the questions:

The National Flag of India is a horizontal tricolour of three equal rectangular panels: India Saffron (Kesari) at the top, White in the middle, and India Green at the bottom. The ratio of the width (height) to the length of the flag is strictly 2 : 3. In the center of the white band is the Ashoka Chakra, rendered in navy blue, containing 24 equally spaced spokes. As explained by Dr. S. Radhakrishnan in the Constituent Assembly, Saffron denotes renunciation, courage, and dedication to service; White denotes the path of light, truth, purity, and non-violence; and Green denotes our connection to the soil, plant life, and material prosperity upon which all life depends. The Ashoka Chakra, adapted from the 3rd-century B.C. Sarnath Lion Capital of Emperor Ashoka, represents the eternal Wheel of the Law (Dharma Chakra), dynamic motion, and the peaceful progress of the nation, while its 24 spokes symbolize round-the-clock advancement and foundational ethical virtues.

topic: Sunset Sky Symbolism in Journey's End
questionText:
Read the following excerpt on Abanindranath Tagore's masterpiece 'Journey's End' and answer the questions that follow:

Painted around 1913 using watercolor and wash on paper, 'Journey's End' by Abanindranath Tagore is universally recognized as one of the supreme masterpieces of pathos (Karuna Rasa) in modern world art. The painting depicts an overburdened, exhausted camel collapsing onto stony desert ground at sunset. Strained to the point of death by an unbearable bundle of cargo tied tightly to its back, the animal slumps forward on its front knees, its long neck stretched out painfully and its mouth half-open, gasping for breath. Its half-closed eye conveys profound weariness, quiet surrender, and release from lifelong suffering. In the background, a dramatic sunset burns with dusky red, ochre, and mauve tones, fading into the dark blue of approaching night. Abanindranath used his signature wash technique—repeatedly soaking the paper in water—to create a weeping, diffused twilight mist that envelops the dying creature, elevating the scene into a timeless universal allegory of exploited human labor and mortal death, conserved in the NGMA, New Delhi.

Question: What does the setting sun and approaching nocturnal darkness in the painting metaphorically signify?

questionText:
Read the following excerpt on Nandalal Bose's masterpiece 'Parthasarthi' and answer the questions that follow:

Painted in 1912 by master artist Nandalal Bose using watercolor and tempera on paper, 'Parthasarthi' (Charioteer of Partha) is a defining masterpiece of modern Indian mythological art. Set in the apocalyptic prelude to the Kurukshetra war from the Mahabharata, the painting portrays Lord Krishna acting as the divine charioteer for the Pandava warrior Arjuna. Krishna is depicted at the front of the war chariot, holding the reins of four spirited white horses with his left hand while raising and blowing the sacred conch shell Panchajanya with his right hand to declare the righteous battle. His celestial face radiates divine composure and majestic authority. Seated reverently behind Krishna in the chariot is warrior prince Arjuna, his mighty bow Gandiva resting beside him, gazing with complete faith and surrender at his divine charioteer. Nandalal uses sweeping calligraphic contours influenced by the Ajanta cave murals to create an atmosphere of heroic righteousness and cosmic destiny, conserved in the National Gallery of Modern Art (NGMA), New Delhi.

Question: In Indian philosophical allegories of the chariot (Kathopanishad), what do the four horses represent?
